name: Mau movement
info: The Mau was a non-violent movement for Samoan independence from colonial rule in the first half of the 20th century, which grew from a resistance on Savai'i in 1908 into a national movement and ended with independence in 1962.

facts.where: Samoa, above all Upolu, Savai'i and the capital Apia in the Western Islands; a separate Mau in Tutuila, American Samoa; leaders exiled to the Marianas and to New Zealand
facts.period: Mau a Pule on Savai'i from 1908; Lauaki and other leaders exiled 1909; New Zealand annexation 1914; O le Mau formed 1926; height of activity in the late 1920s and early 1930s; Black Saturday in December 1929; truce 12 March 1930; Samoan Fono opened 1936; independence 1962
facts.figures: Lauaki Namulau'ulu Mamoe, founder of the Mau a Pule; Olaf Frederick Nelson, merchant of mixed Swedish and Samoan heritage; Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III, paramount chief killed on Black Saturday; Luafalemana Moeono Taele, matua of Falefa; Alfred Smyth and Edwin Gurr, part-European leaders; Samuel Sailele Ripley, leader of the American Samoa Mau
facts.outcome: the movement's efforts ultimately resulted in the political independence of Samoa in 1962; in 2002 New Zealand's Prime Minister apologised for the colonial treatment of Samoans; the American Samoa Mau was totally suppressed by the United States

t: Mau means 'resolute' in Samoan, and its motto was Samoa mo Samoa (Samoa for the Samoans); it built on village committees of chiefs and talking men, and by the mid- to late 1920s around 85% of Samoans were involved in open resistance.

Its methods were boycotts, refusal to pay taxes, picketing and mass arrests in which prisoners demanded trial, and on Black Saturday in December 1929 New Zealand military police fired on a procession in Apia, killing Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III among others.

Western Samoa became independent in 1962, with Tupua Tamasese Meaole, brother of the slain Mau leader, as co-head of state; in 2002 New Zealand's Prime Minister Helen Clark apologised for the colonial treatment of Samoans.
dyk: When the Mau were arrested in such numbers that there were too few jail cells, the prisoners came and went as they pleased; one group held in a three-sided 'cell' facing the ocean swam away to tend their gardens and visit their families.
ev: A dispute between the German colonial administration and the Samoan Council of Chiefs over a native-owned copra business leads to the formation of the Mau a Pule on Savai'i
Lauaki and the other senior leaders of the Mau a Pule are exiled to the German colonies in the Marianas
At the outbreak of the First World War, New Zealand forces annex Western Samoa without German opposition
After Olaf Nelson's lobbying in Wellington, two public meetings in Apia form the Samoan League, O le Mau
New Zealand military police fire on a procession in Apia on Black Saturday, killing Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III
A truce is declared on 12 March, with the male Mau members keeping their right to non-cooperation
A Samoan Fono with elected representatives is opened at Mulinu'u after the election of a Labour Government in New Zealand

sections.background:
The history of the Mau movement can be seen as beginning in the 19th century, with European contact and the advance of Britain, the United States and Germany, each vying for control of the Pacific nation. Samoa became German Samoa (1900–1914). In 1908 a dispute arose between the German colonial administration and the Malo o Samoa, the Samoan Council of Chiefs, over the establishment of a copra business owned and controlled by native Samoans. It led to the formation of a resistance movement, the Mau a Pule, on Savai'i by Lauaki Namulau'ulu Mamoe, a leader from Safotulafai who was deposed by the German Governor, Wilhelm Solf.

Solf deposed members of the Malo o Samoa and called in two German warships as a show of strength. He then arranged a 'peace talk' on a German ship, on condition that Lauaki first disperse his army, and Lauaki and some of the chiefs were betrayed there. In 1909 Lauaki and the other senior leaders were exiled to the Marianas, where they stayed until 1914. Many died before returning, and Lauaki died on the way back to Samoa in 1915. In 1914, at the start of the First World War, New Zealand forces annexed Western Samoa, unopposed by the Germans.

Military rule by New Zealand continued after the war. An influenza epidemic then killed some 7,500 Samoans, around 22 per cent of the population, after the ship SS Talune was allowed to dock at Apia with its crew and passengers obviously sick. No attempt was made to contain the spread, whereas American Samoa, which had taken quarantine precautions, had no deaths. This catastrophe laid a new foundation for discontent with an administration many Samoans already thought incompetent and dishonest.
sections.aims:
The Mau was a non-violent movement for Samoan independence from colonial rule. In Samoan the word means 'resolute' or 'resolved', in the sense of 'opinion', 'unwavering', 'to be decided' or 'testimony', and also denotes firm strength. Its motto was the words Samoa mo Samoa, 'Samoa for the Samoans'. Its petition to the New Zealand Government quoted an ancient Samoan proverb: 'We are moved by love, but never driven by intimidation.' Supporters wore a uniform of a navy blue lavalava with a white stripe, which the colonial administration later banned.

The grievances were those of an administration perceived as incompetent and dishonest, together with the slow and deliberate erosion of traditional Samoan social structures by successive administrators and a general failure to understand and respect Samoan culture. Olaf Frederick Nelson, one of the leaders, was frustrated by the exclusion of native and part-Samoans from governance, and in 1926 he went to Wellington to lobby the New Zealand government for increased self-rule.

The movement's methods were forms of non-cooperation. Members neglected the compulsory weekly search for the rhinoceros beetle, an enemy of the coconut palm, which threatened the copra industry; when a per-capita quota was imposed, many villages bred the insects in tightly woven baskets instead of collecting them. Later the Mau boycotted imported goods, refused to pay taxes and picketed stores in Apia to prevent the payment of customs. In 1931 news of the Indian independence movement reached Samoa and partly inspired the Mau.
sections.events:
When the Minister for External Affairs, William Nosworthy, promised to visit Samoa and then postponed his trip, Nelson organised two public meetings in Apia, attended by hundreds, and the Samoan League, O le Mau, was formed in 1926. It published the Samoa Guardian as its mouthpiece. In 1927 the administrator, George Richardson, changed the law to allow the deportation of Europeans or part-Europeans charged with fomenting unrest; Nelson was later exiled with two other part-European leaders, Alfred Smyth and Edwin Gurr. A joint select committee admitted that a very substantial proportion of Samoans had joined the Mau, enough to paralyse the functions of government.

Richardson sent a warship and a force of 70 marines. About 400 Mau members were arrested, but others gave themselves up in such numbers that cells ran short, and those arrested demanded trial and then refused to enter pleas, rejecting the court's jurisdiction. The next administrator, Stephen Allen, replaced the marines with special New Zealand police and targeted the leaders. Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III was imprisoned for six months for non-payment of taxes.

On Black Saturday, late in December 1929, New Zealand military police fired on a procession assembled to welcome home Alfred Smyth. Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III, calling for peace with his back to the police, was shot. Eight Samoans died that day, three later, and about 50 were wounded; one policeman was clubbed to death. Marines were sent in January 1930, a Samoan boy of 16 was shot dead running away, and a truce was declared on 12 March 1930.
sections.people:
The Mau's support came from the matai, the heads of families in Samoa's traditional structure, who used family and chiefly title connections to gather it. Each village that joined formed a committee of chiefs and 'talking men'; these committees became the basic element of an alternative system of governance. To win Savai'i's orators, the Tumua of Upolu sailed in a fleet of canoes under Luafalemana Moeono Taele, matua of Falefa, who had resigned from the administration's police force to join the Mau. Moeono recalled Falefa's support for the Mau a Pule and so persuaded Asiata and the assembled Pule to join.

Samoans of mixed parentage, facing discrimination from both cultures, also played a key role. Olaf Frederick Nelson was a merchant of mixed Swedish and Samoan heritage, the richest man in Samoa and well travelled; classified as a European, he considered himself Samoan 'by birth, blood, and sentiment'. He had lost a child, his mother, sister, only brother and a sister-in-law to the influenza epidemic. Alfred Smyth and Edwin Gurr were also part-European leaders.

Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III, one of the paramount chiefs of Samoa, led the movement after Nelson's exile. As he lay dying he is said to have told his followers: 'My blood has been spilt for Samoa, I am proud to give it. Do not dream of avenging it, as it was spilt in peace. If I die, peace must be maintained at any price.' After Black Saturday the Women's Mau emerged within days, as men hid from the administration. Women hid and protected the men and carried on writing letters of complaint and organising protests; Nelson telegraphed New Zealand's Labour Party that Samoan women were organising a movement 'unparalleled in Samoan history'.
sections.outcomes:
Nelson returned to Samoa in May 1933 after five years in exile in New Zealand. The administrator, General Hart, demanded that he be excluded from any fono with the Mau leadership, and the Mau insisted he should be one of its delegates. On 15 November 1933 police raided the Mau's headquarters at Vaimoso and Nelson's residence at Tuaefu, and eight chiefs at a conference of 100 were arrested, with seven more at Savai'i a week later. Six months after his return Nelson was convicted of three charges of being connected to the Mau and sentenced to ten more years of exile and eight months of imprisonment in New Zealand.

The treatment of Samoans had become a contentious issue in some New Zealand electorates in the general election of 1935, which Labour won. Nelson's exile was cut short in 1936. The election of a Labour Government in New Zealand that year was a turning point: repression was relaxed, and a Samoan Parliament with elected representatives was opened at Mulinu'u on 30 September 1936. There were further acts of civil disobedience, including a sit-in in parliament over the payment of the representatives. Nelson helped sign a co-operation agreement between Samoan leaders and the administration and was elected to the Legislative Council in 1938 and 1941.

In 1946 a Fono of district representatives rejected a Trusteeship Agreement put forward by New Zealand, stating a desire for self-government. When Western Samoa became independent in 1962, Tupua Tamasese Meaole, younger brother and successor of the slain Mau leader, became its first co-head of state with Malietoa Tanumafili II. Fiamē Mata'afa Faumuina Mulinu'u II, son of the Mau leader Mata'afa Faumuina Fiame Mulinu'u I, became the first Prime Minister.
sections.legacy:
The success of the Mau in gathering national support showed that fa'a Samoa was still strong despite colonialism. Its efforts ultimately resulted in Samoa's political independence in 1962, though the height of its activity in the Western Islands was in the late 1920s and early 1930s. In July 1997 the Samoa Constitution was amended to change the country's name to Samoa, officially the Independent State of Samoa. Scholars have called the women's movement that emerged after Black Saturday a successful one.

In 2002, at Apia during the 40th anniversary of independence, New Zealand's Prime Minister Helen Clark made an unprecedented move and apologised to Samoa for New Zealand's treatment of Samoans in the colonial era. The apology covered the influenza epidemic, the shooting of unarmed Mau protesters by New Zealand police in 1929 and the banishing of matai from their homes.

A Mau also arose in American Samoa, in opposition to the United States annexation of the eastern islands in 1899. In the 1920s on Tutuila it signed petitions and resisted the taxation of copra, in an open affront to the American Navy. Its leader, Samuel Sailele Ripley of Leone, was barred from disembarking on his return from California and never allowed home; he later became mayor of Richmond, California. A committee sent in 1930 reported in favour of the American position, and the movement was totally suppressed, though its influence continued to be felt. A Samoan hip hop group founded in 1990 took the name The Mau and the motto Samoa Mo Samoa.

summary: The Mau was a non-violent Samoan movement against colonial rule that grew from the Mau a Pule of 1908 on Savai'i into a national movement in the 1920s, led by chiefs and part-European leaders. New Zealand police killed Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III and others on Black Saturday in 1929, and Samoa became independent in 1962.
references: Michael J. Field, Mau: Samoa's struggle against New Zealand oppression (Reed Publishing, 1984)
notes: Date conflict: the lede says Black Saturday was 28 December 1929, the section heading and text say 29 December. I wrote 'late in December 1929' in the text and only the year in events.

Death toll conflict: the lede says 'up to 11 Samoans were killed'; the section says eight died, three would later die, about 50 wounded, one policeman clubbed to death. I used the section's figures (eight, three later), which sum to the lede's 11.
Influenza epidemic: the history section dates it 1919, the apology section 1918. I left out the year.
Start 1908 (the dispute and Mau a Pule; the lede says 'early 1900s'), circa true. End 1962 (independence); the article says the height of activity was late 1920s-early 1930s.

Left out Colonel Logan's destroyed telegram and the article's remark that he hated Americans (a claim of character); left out the article's claim that Samoans were most susceptible to minor European diseases.

Tamasese's last words are quoted as the article gives them, with 'is said to have told'; the article's own sentence 'In the Mau's darkest period came its finest hour' is a verdict and was left out. It also says reports of the massacre are sketchy because the official cover-up was so effective; not used.
The truce 'male Mau members returned to their homes'; the article says another child was killed by marines before the truce (I wrote only the 16-year-old, who was shot earlier).
Left out: the Hawaiian meaning of mau, the article's account of the German governor's trap in detail, Allen's claim of a riot of 2,000 Mau and the raid on Tamasese's village, and the 'See also'.
The article's text 'Mau leader Taisi Olaf Nelson' appears in the Women's Mau passage; I used Nelson's usual name.

References left empty for the editor; the article's Further reading names Field, Mau: Samoa's struggle against New Zealand oppression (Reed, 1984) and Chapell, 'The Forgotten Mau' (Pacific Historical Review, 2000).
